# Case: Tesla Model S with Autopilot (Williston, Florida, 2016)

Source: NTSB Highway Accident Report HAR-17/02. This is a description of the system and its use before the crash. It does not include the investigation findings.

## System
A 2015 Tesla Model S has Autopilot, a SAE Level 2 partial driving automation feature. It combines Traffic-Aware Cruise Control (TACC) and Autosteer (lane keeping). The driver stays responsible for driving and monitoring the road.

## Main parts
- Sensors: a forward-facing camera, a forward-facing radar and ultrasonic sensors.
- Vision processing: a camera-based system detects lane markings and objects ahead.
- TACC: holds a speed set by the driver, slows down for a vehicle ahead in the same lane, and speeds up again when the lane is clear.
- Autosteer: keeps the vehicle centered in its lane using lane markings and the vehicle ahead.
- Forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking are available as separate features.
- Driver monitoring: the system checks that the driver's hands are on the steering wheel by sensing steering torque, and shows visual and audible alerts if no hands are detected for a period of time.

## People
- The driver sets the cruising speed, turns Autopilot on, and is told to keep hands on the wheel and watch the road.
- Other road users include cars, large trucks crossing or joining the road, and motorcyclists.

## Operating context
Autopilot is intended mainly for highways with limited access, in good visibility. Drivers can also turn it on for other roads, such as divided highways with cross traffic at intersections.

You are a safety analyst doing obstacle analysis on a goal model.

An obstacle is a condition that prevents a goal from being satisfied.
For EACH goal below, propose obstacles. Use these guide words to search:
- omission: the system or an actor does not do something it should
- commission: it does something it should not
- too early / too late: it acts at the wrong time

Also check these obstacle types:
- non-information: an actor never gets information it needs
- wrong belief: an actor assumes something about the world that can be false
- inaccuracy: information is imprecise, unstable or out of date
- unavailability: a needed agent or resource is missing or switched off

Do not only think about sensor or hardware faults. Also think about what people and other road users
actually do (for example a pedestrian in an unexpected place, an operator who looks away or relies too
much on the system), how the system classifies and tracks objects, and what it does with uncertain
detections (for example ignoring or suppressing them).

For every obstacle, name the hidden premise it violates: the assumption that someone
thought was too obvious to write down.

Return at most 10 obstacles in total, ranked from most to least important for safety.

Reply with JSON only, in this shape:
{"obstacles": [{"id": "o1", "goal_id": "g1", "guide_word": "omission",
                "text": "...", "violated_premise": "..."}]}

requirements.text: The system shall ensure that the elapsed time between collision prediction and issuance of the emergency‑brake command does not exceed 200 ms under all operating conditions, and shall verify that the command is issued at least 500 ms before the predicted time‑to‑collision.

The system shall detect any vehicle that enters the host lane within a forward range of 120 m using a fused camera‑radar‑ultrasonic sensor suite, and shall trigger the following‑distance controller within 0.2 s of detection.

The system shall determine driver hand presence by requiring agreement of at least two independent modalities (steering‑torque sensor and capacitive hand‑presence sensor or driver‑monitoring camera); if both indicate hands off for more than 1 s, a visual and audible warning shall be issued.

The system shall include objects detected with a confidence score of 0.3 or higher in the collision‑avoidance risk assessment, weighting risk proportionally to confidence, and shall not suppress collision warnings solely because of low confidence.

The system shall cross‑validate radar distance measurements with camera‑based depth estimates; any radar reading that deviates by more than 10 % from the camera estimate during heavy rain shall be discarded and the following‑distance algorithm shall use only the validated data.

The system shall apply a lane‑detection sanity check that requires a detected lane marking to be continuous for at least 15 m and not intersect the bounding box of any vehicle detected ahead; if a conflict is found, lane‑keeping shall be suppressed and the vehicle shall rely on object‑avoidance steering.

The system shall continuously estimate the appropriate maximum speed based on road type, posted speed limit, curvature, and weather, and shall limit the driver‑set cruising speed to no more than 5 km/h above that estimate; if the driver exceeds it, the system shall automatically reduce speed to the estimated maximum.

The system shall display a persistent on‑screen message and emit an audible alert stating “Autopilot is limited to limited‑access highways; it does not control intersections” whenever the vehicle approaches a road segment with a crossing or signalized intersection, and shall disable Autopilot if the driver attempts to engage it in that context.

The system shall perform a self‑diagnostic check of the forward‑facing camera lens before Autopilot activation using built‑in illumination and image‑clarity metrics; if obstruction exceeds a predefined threshold, Autopilot shall be disabled and a warning shall be presented to the driver.

The system shall monitor lateral motion vectors of adjacent vehicles and, when a vehicle within 30 m exhibits a lateral velocity greater than 0.5 m/s toward the host lane, shall generate a provisional path adjustment or driver warning within 0.3 s, regardless of whether a turn signal is present.
